title: Pigeonhole Bound: Linear Upper Threshold
content: The pigeonhole bound for k-way coincidences is (k-1)·d + 1: with this many people, at least k must share a birthday. This is the worst-case guarantee from the pigeonhole principle. The three theorems prove the bound value equals itself (tautological but documents the formula), and that it grows linearly in both d and k. The key contrast with the probabilistic threshold n_k ~ d^{(k-1)/k}: the pigeonhole bound is linear (exponent 1 in d), while the 50%-probability threshold has exponent (k-1)/k < 1.
mathContext: Pigeonhole bound: $(k-1) \cdot d + 1$ people guarantee $k$-way coincidence. Contrast: probabilistic threshold $n_k \sim (k! \cdot d^{k-1})^{1/k}$ grows as $d^{(k-1)/k}$. Ratio: pigeonhole/threshold $\approx d^{1/(k-1)}/k!^{1/k}$, diverges as $d \to \infty$ for fixed $k \geq 2$.

title: Scaling Exponent (k-1)/k and Concrete Values
content: scalingExponent k = (k-1)/k is the growth exponent for the k-way birthday threshold. The file proves: non-negativity (always ≥ 0), strict sublinearity (< 1 for k ≥ 1), monotone increasing in k, and three concrete values: scalingExponent 2 = 1/2 (square root law), scalingExponent 3 = 2/3, scalingExponent 4 = 3/4. The exponent increases toward 1 as k→∞, interpolating between the trivial case (k=1, exponent 0, threshold = constant 1) and the pigeonhole case (k→∞, exponent 1, threshold linear in d).
mathContext: $\alpha_k = \frac{k-1}{k}$, so $n_k \sim d^{\alpha_k}$. Monotone: $k_1 \leq k_2 \Rightarrow \alpha_{k_1} \leq \alpha_{k_2}$. Values: $\alpha_2 = 1/2$, $\alpha_3 = 2/3$, $\alpha_4 = 3/4$, $\alpha_k \to 1$ as $k \to \infty$.

title: Threshold Power Formula: k! · d^{k-1}
content: thresholdPower k d = (k! · d^{k-1} : ℝ) works with the k-th power n_k^k to avoid fractional exponents. This makes monotonicity and comparison proofs algebraically clean: thresholdPower_pos, thresholdPower_mono_d, and thresholdPower_mono_k are all proved via positivity/monotonicity of multiplication and rpow. The factorial factor k! captures the combinatorial growth of coincidence patterns: among k people, there are k! orderings of their birthdays, and all k! of them must be distinct.
mathContext: $n_k^k = k! \cdot d^{k-1}$. Taking $k$-th roots: $n_k = (k! \cdot d^{k-1})^{1/k} = (k!)^{1/k} \cdot d^{(k-1)/k}$. By Stirling: $(k!)^{1/k} \approx k/e$, so the prefactor grows as $k/e$ for large $k$.

title: Classical Recovery: k=2,3,4 Formulas and 365-Day Examples
content: threshold_k2/k3/k4 compute the threshold power for the first three non-trivial cases: n₂² = 2d (square-root birthday), n₃³ = 6d², n₄⁴ = 24d³. These are proved by unfolding thresholdPower and simplifying Nat.factorial. The comparison theorems show that for d ≥ 2 (k=2) or d ≥ 1 (k=3), the probabilistic threshold is strictly smaller than the pigeonhole bound — confirming the birthday problem effect. Concrete 365-day examples: thresholdPower 2 365 = 730 (so n₂ ≈ √730 ≈ 27 people), thresholdPower 3 365 = 6·365² = 798,150.
mathContext: For $d=365$: $n_2 = \sqrt{730} \approx 27$, $n_3 = (6 \cdot 365^2)^{1/3} \approx 92$. Comparison: $n_2 \approx 27 \ll (2-1) \cdot 365 + 1 = 366$ (pigeonhole). Birthday problem: exact $P(\text{no shared birthday}) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 - i/365)$, threshold when $< 1/2$.

title: Exponent Approaches 1: Convergence to the Pigeonhole Bound
content: As k → ∞, the scaling exponent (k-1)/k → 1, meaning the threshold approaches linear growth in d (the pigeonhole bound). The proof gives an explicit convergence rate: for (k-1)/k > 1 - ε, it suffices to take k > 1/ε. This is the Archimedean property applied to show that for any ε > 0, eventually all k-way coincidences behave like the worst-case pigeonhole scenario. The theorem bridges the probabilistic and combinatorial regimes.
